blocks.text: By the end of this guide, you should be able to:
Inspect spinal alignment, posture and deformities.
Palpate for tenderness, step deformities and muscle spasm.
Assess spinal range of motion.
Perform appropriate nerve root tension tests.
Examine the upper or lower limbs neurologically when indicated.
Recognise scoliosis, kyphosis, lordosis and other spinal abnormalities.
Identify red flags suggesting spinal cord compression, cauda equina syndrome, infection, malignancy or fracture.
Present your findings in a structured OSCE format.
The vertebral column consists of:
Cervical spine: C1–C7; supports the head and permits neck movement.
Thoracic spine: T1–T12; articulates with the ribs.
Lumbar spine: L1–L5; bears much of the body's weight.
Sacrum: Five fused vertebrae.
Coccyx: Usually four fused vertebral segments, with variation.
The spinal cord generally terminates around the L1–L2 vertebral level in adults. Below this level, lumbar and sacral nerve roots continue as the cauda equina.

items: Cervical lordosis

blocks.text: A normal inward curve of the neck.

items: Thoracic kyphosis

blocks.text: A normal outward curve of the thoracic spine.

items: Lumbar lordosis

blocks.text: A normal inward curve of the lower back.
These curves are physiological. The examination aims to identify excessive, reduced or abnormal curvature rather than assuming that all curvature is pathological.
Examination couch.
Goniometer or inclinometer if required.
Reflex hammer.
Cotton wool and an appropriate sensory-testing instrument.
Disposable neurotip where indicated.
Examination gown or drape.

“Good morning. My name is … I have been asked to examine your spine. I will inspect your back, feel along the spine, assess its movements and, if indicated, examine the nerves supplying your arms or legs. Some movements may cause discomfort, so please tell me if you experience pain. Is that alright?”
Then:
Confirm the patient's identity.
Explain the examination and obtain consent.
Ask about pain and any recent injury.
Provide privacy and expose the spine appropriately.
Wash your hands.
Position the patient standing initially, if safe.
Ensure the patient can sit or lie down comfortably when needed.

Safety point: If a spinal fracture or unstable injury is suspected, do not ask the patient to bend, twist or perform provocative manoeuvres. Maintain appropriate spinal precautions and arrange urgent assessment.
Ask about:
Site and onset of pain.
Duration and progression.
Radiation to the arm, buttock or leg.
Aggravating and relieving factors.
Stiffness and restriction of movement.
Numbness, tingling or weakness.
Gait disturbance or falls.
Bladder or bowel dysfunction.
Saddle or perineal sensory disturbance.
Fever, recent infection or immunosuppression.
History of malignancy or unexplained weight loss.
Trauma, osteoporosis or prolonged corticosteroid use.
Previous spinal surgery or similar episodes.

blocks.text: These symptoms require interpretation in context. A normal physical examination does not reliably exclude serious spinal pathology.
Observe the patient standing, if safe.
Inspect from the front, side and back.
Look for:
Abnormal posture.
Unequal shoulder heights.
Pelvic tilt or asymmetry.
Abnormal spinal curvature.
Muscle wasting.
Scars from previous surgery.
Skin lesions or swelling.
Use of walking aids.
Antalgic posture or difficulty standing upright.
Observe the patient's gait if appropriate, noting stride length, balance and symmetry.
Normal finding: The patient stands comfortably, with symmetrical shoulders and pelvis, normal spinal alignment and no obvious deformity.
Abnormal finding: Asymmetry, abnormal curvature, guarding or an antalgic posture may suggest spinal or musculoskeletal pathology.

content_groups.group_title: Step 2: Inspect spinal alignment and deformities

items: A. Scoliosis

blocks.text: Lateral curvature of the spine, often accompanied by vertebral rotation and asymmetry of the shoulders, waist or rib cage.

items: B. Excessive kyphosis

blocks.text: Increased posterior convexity of the thoracic spine, which may occur with vertebral compression fractures, osteoporosis or other spinal disorders.

items: C. Excessive lordosis

blocks.text: Increased inward curvature, sometimes associated with pelvic tilt, pregnancy or certain neuromuscular conditions.
This is useful when scoliosis is suspected.
Ask the patient to stand with feet together.
Ask them to bend forward slowly, allowing the arms to hang down.
Inspect the back from behind.
Look for a rib hump or asymmetry of the paraspinal muscles.
A positive finding suggests vertebral rotation associated with scoliosis, but does not establish the cause or severity. Formal assessment may require a scoliometer and standing spinal radiographs.
Ask the patient to indicate any painful area before you begin.
Palpate gently along the spinal midline and surrounding muscles, provided there is no suspicion of an unstable injury.
Palpate the spinous processes from the cervical region to the sacrum as relevant.
Normal: No focal bony tenderness.
Abnormal: Focal vertebral tenderness may suggest fracture, infection, tumour or other local pathology.
Palpate the muscles alongside the vertebral column.
Normal: No significant tenderness, spasm or palpable abnormality.
Abnormal: Muscle tenderness or spasm may accompany mechanical back pain, but is not specific to a particular diagnosis.
Gently assess for a palpable step where clinically appropriate.
A step deformity may indicate vertebral displacement or another structural abnormality. Avoid repeated palpation if significant trauma or instability is suspected.
If the history suggests sacroiliac or inflammatory spinal disease, examine the relevant region and perform appropriate additional tests.
Important: Do not repeatedly press hard on the spine in an attempt to provoke pain. Your examination should be systematic and gentle.
Ask the patient to perform active movements within a comfortable range. Observe the range, pain and any compensatory movement.
Assess:
Flexion — chin towards the chest.
Extension — looking upwards.
Rotation — turning the head to each side.
Lateral flexion — bringing the ear towards the shoulder.
Normal finding: Movements are reasonably full and symmetrical without significant pain.
Abnormal findings: Restricted movement, pain, muscle spasm or asymmetry may indicate musculoskeletal disease, degenerative changes or other pathology.
Do not force neck movement when cervical instability, fracture or serious neurological pathology is suspected.
Thoracic movement is assessed partly through trunk rotation and side bending, recognising that rib-cage mechanics limit movement.
Assess:
Trunk rotation to each side.
Lateral flexion.
Thoracic posture and extension where appropriate.
Abnormal finding: Painful restriction, deformity or marked asymmetry warrants further assessment.
Assess:
Flexion — bending forward.
Extension — leaning backwards.
Lateral flexion — sliding one hand down each side of the thigh.
Rotation — gentle trunk rotation if appropriate.
Observe for restricted movement, pain, asymmetry and compensatory hip movement.
Normal finding: Lumbar movements are reasonably full and symmetrical, without significant pain.
Abnormal finding: Restricted or painful movement may accompany mechanical back pain, degenerative disease, inflammatory disease or other spinal pathology.
Schober's test assesses lumbar flexion and is sometimes used when ankylosing spondylitis or axial spondyloarthritis is suspected.
In a traditional modified technique:
Identify the lumbosacral landmark, usually around the level of the posterior superior iliac spines.
Mark a point approximately 10 cm above and 5 cm below the reference point.
Ask the patient to bend forward maximally, keeping the knees straight if comfortable.
Re-measure the distance between the marks.
The increase in distance provides an estimate of lumbar flexion. Reduced expansion may suggest restricted lumbar mobility.
Interpret the result according to the technique used and local reference values; Schober's test alone cannot diagnose axial spondyloarthritis.

content_groups.group_title: Step 5: Assess for nerve root irritation

blocks.text: Perform these tests when indicated by the history and initial examination.

items: prepakproducts.com

blocks.text: Purpose: Assesses whether raising the straight leg reproduces symptoms associated with lumbosacral nerve root irritation.
Technique:
Position the patient supine.
Keep the knee extended.
Raise the leg slowly by flexing the hip.
Ask whether the manoeuvre reproduces their usual symptoms.
Note the angle and distribution of the pain.
Interpretation:
Reproduction of familiar radiating pain down the leg, particularly below the knee, supports nerve root irritation.
Isolated hamstring tightness or back pain is not considered a typical positive radicular SLR.
A negative test does not exclude radiculopathy.
A positive test is commonly described when familiar radicular pain occurs at approximately 30–70 degrees of hip flexion, although the angle alone is not diagnostic.
Raise the unaffected leg while observing whether this reproduces radicular pain in the opposite symptomatic leg.
A positive crossed SLR is less sensitive but can be more specific for a lumbar disc herniation causing nerve root irritation.
This may be useful when upper lumbar nerve root irritation is suspected.

With the patient positioned appropriately, gently flex the knee and extend the hip, observing whether familiar anterior thigh pain is reproduced. Use caution in patients with hip pathology or recent injury.
A spinal examination is incomplete when neurological symptoms are present unless you assess the relevant limb nerves.
For suspected lumbar radiculopathy, examine lower-limb power, sensation and reflexes. For cervical symptoms, examine the upper limbs and consider signs of spinal cord involvement.

rows: Medial leg to dorsum of foot, with overlap
Dorsum of foot near great toe
No consistently reliable routine deep tendon reflex

blocks.text: Dermatomes and myotomes overlap, so individual findings must be interpreted as a pattern.
Assess gait, heel walking, toe walking and relevant muscle power only if safe.
For cervical spine pathology, assess:
Shoulder abduction.
Elbow flexion and extension.
Wrist extension.
Finger flexion and abduction.
Sensation in relevant dermatomal distributions.
Biceps, brachioradialis and triceps reflexes.
Also look for possible cervical myelopathy, including gait disturbance, hand clumsiness, hyperreflexia and pathological reflexes when clinically indicated.
Critical distinction: Radiculopathy affects a nerve root, while myelopathy reflects spinal cord dysfunction. Progressive weakness, gait changes or signs of cord involvement require urgent assessment.
Depending on the presentation, an examiner may expect you to mention:
Gait assessment: Look for antalgia, imbalance, foot drop or spasticity.
Heel and toe walking: Screens selected lower-limb motor functions.
Neurological examination: Essential when pain radiates or neurological symptoms are reported.
Hip examination: Hip pathology can present as lower back or buttock pain.
Peripheral vascular examination: Consider if symptoms suggest vascular claudication.
Examination of sacroiliac joints: When inflammatory disease or sacroiliac pathology is suspected.
Do not perform every special test routinely. Choose tests according to the history and initial findings.

subsections.subsection_title: Red flags you must never miss

items: Cauda equina syndrome

blocks.text: New urinary retention or altered urinary sensation, saddle sensory loss, bowel dysfunction or progressive bilateral leg weakness may indicate cauda equina compression. Arrange emergency assessment and urgent MRI where indicated.

items: Spinal cord compression

blocks.text: Progressive limb weakness, gait disturbance, a sensory level, or new bladder or bowel dysfunction may indicate cord compression. Urgent assessment is required.

items: Spinal infection

blocks.text: Back pain with fever, immunosuppression, recent bacteraemia, intravenous drug use or recent spinal procedures should raise suspicion of vertebral osteomyelitis or spinal epidural abscess. Fever may be absent.

items: Malignancy or fracture

blocks.text: Consider malignancy with a relevant cancer history or other concerning features. Consider fracture following significant trauma or even minor trauma in a patient with osteoporosis or prolonged corticosteroid exposure.

Red flags do not always mean serious disease is present, but they require appropriate assessment. Do not rely on a single negative symptom or a normal bedside examination to exclude a serious condition.
“On inspection, the patient has normal spinal alignment with preserved physiological curves and no scoliosis, kyphosis, abnormal lordosis, scars or muscle wasting.
There is no midline or paraspinal tenderness, palpable step deformity or significant muscle spasm.
Cervical, thoracic and lumbar movements are reasonably full and symmetrical without significant pain.
Where indicated, neurological examination of the relevant limbs reveals normal power, sensation and reflexes, with no focal neurological deficit.
Overall, there are no significant abnormalities detected on the spinal examination.”
Only include the spinal regions and neurological findings that you actually assessed.

content_groups.group_title: Scenario A: Mechanical lower back pain

blocks.text: “There is restricted and painful lumbar movement, with paraspinal muscle tenderness but no focal neurological deficit on examination. The findings may be consistent with mechanical lower back pain, subject to the clinical history and exclusion of red flags.”

“The patient has lower back pain radiating down the leg, with reproduction of familiar radicular symptoms on straight leg raise. There is associated sensory disturbance in a relevant distribution. These findings suggest lumbar nerve root irritation. I would complete a focused neurological examination and assess for red flags.”

“There is lateral spinal curvature with asymmetry of the shoulders and waist. A rib prominence is present on forward bending. These findings suggest scoliosis. I would assess the degree of deformity and arrange further evaluation where indicated.”

content_groups.group_title: Scenario D: Possible spinal cord compression

blocks.text: “The patient has spinal pain with progressive limb weakness, gait disturbance and abnormal neurological findings. These features raise concern for spinal cord compression, requiring urgent specialist assessment and appropriate imaging.”

content_groups.group_title: Scenario E: Possible cauda equina syndrome

blocks.text: “The patient has lower back pain with new bladder dysfunction and saddle sensory disturbance. This is concerning for cauda equina syndrome and requires emergency assessment and urgent investigation.”

subsections.subsection_title: Investigations an examiner may ask about

rows: Selected suspected fractures, deformities or structural abnormalities
Suspected spinal cord or nerve root compression, infection, malignancy or other soft-tissue pathology
Detailed assessment of bony injury or when CT is the appropriate available alternative
Full blood count and inflammatory markers
Suspected infection, inflammation or malignancy, depending on the presentation
Selected persistent or unexplained neurological deficits

blocks.text: Imaging is not routinely necessary for uncomplicated, non-specific lower back pain without concerning features. Investigation should be guided by clinical findings and the suspected diagnosis.
Failing to inspect the spine from the front, side and back.
Missing abnormal spinal curvature.
Performing painful movements before assessing for possible injury.
Forgetting to palpate the midline and paraspinal muscles.
Failing to distinguish spinal pain from radicular pain.
Performing a straight leg raise without asking whether the patient's familiar symptoms are reproduced.
Omitting neurological examination when limb symptoms are present.
Missing bladder, bowel or saddle sensory symptoms.
Forgetting to examine gait and function when safe.
Failing to state the urgency of suspected cord compression or cauda equina syndrome.

blocks.text: Key takeaway: A good spine examination combines inspection, palpation, movement and a targeted neurological assessment. The most important clinical skill is recognising when apparently ordinary back pain may represent a serious neurological or spinal condition.
